title: Airports and Flying
subtitle: Notices, jobs, a first flight and a pilot

parts.title: Notices and messages
parts.instructions: For each notice, choose what it means.
notices: AIRPORT SHUTTLE: Buses to the terminal leave every twenty minutes from the main station. Tickets are cheaper if you buy them online before you travel.
SECURITY: Please take all liquids out of your bag and put them in a clear plastic bag. Laptops must also be placed in a separate tray.
LOST LUGGAGE: If your suitcase does not arrive, go to the desk next to the carousels. Staff will ask you to fill in a short form.
GATE CHANGE: Flight BA204 to Madrid will now leave from Gate 14 instead of Gate 9. Passengers should go there immediately.
LONG-STAY PARKING: Leave your car for up to two weeks at a special price. Booking is necessary and must be done at least a day before.

parts.title: Jobs at the airport
parts.instructions: Read what each person is looking for. Match each person to the best text. There are three extra texts.

people.text: Hamid enjoys talking to people and would like a job where he helps travellers who are lost or confused. He does not want to work outdoors.
Petra loves machines and wants to work with her hands. She would like to repair engines and make sure planes are safe to fly.
Joon speaks four languages and wants to travel the world while working. He is happy to look after passengers during long flights.
Elsa is good at cooking and would like to prepare meals for a large number of people each day, preferably in a place that is open early.
Dmitri is very calm and organised. He wants a job where he decides which planes can land and take off, and which direction they should take.

texts.title: Cabin Crew
texts.text: Look after passengers on board. Languages are very useful, and you will visit many countries.

texts.title: Baggage Handler
texts.text: Load and unload suitcases. Heavy lifting, outdoors in all weather.

texts.title: Aircraft Engineer
texts.text: Check and repair engines. Technical training provided.

texts.title: Air Traffic Controller
texts.text: Direct planes in the sky and on the runway. Must stay calm under pressure.

texts.title: Airport Chef
texts.text: Prepare breakfast, lunch and dinner for hundreds of staff. The kitchen opens at 5 a.m.

texts.title: Security Officer
texts.text: Check bags and passengers before they enter the departure area.

texts.title: Information Desk Assistant
texts.text: Answer questions and help passengers find their way around the terminal. Indoor work.

texts.title: Pilot
texts.text: Fly large planes. Long training and many exams.

parts.title: My first flight
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
I was twelve when I flew for the first time. My parents had saved money for two years so that we could visit my grandmother in Canada, and I could hardly sleep for a week before the trip.

At the airport, everything seemed enormous. There were so many people, signs and screens that I held my father's hand tightly. When we reached the departure area, a security officer asked me to take off my shoes. I felt embarrassed, but my sister, who had flown before, laughed and told me it was normal.

The moment the plane started to move, my stomach felt strange. We rushed along the runway, and suddenly the ground disappeared. I looked out of the window and saw the whole city getting smaller, like a model. I forgot my fear immediately.

The flight lasted nine hours, which seemed endless. I watched three films, ate two meals, and finally slept for a little while. When we landed, my grandmother was waiting with a huge sign with my name on it. Now I am not afraid of flying at all. In fact, I want to become a pilot one day.

questions.prompt: Why could the writer hardly sleep before the trip?
options: He was excited about the journey
He was worried about the cost
He had a bad cold that week
questions.explanation: He could hardly sleep because he was excited.

questions.prompt: How did the writer feel when asked to take off his shoes?
questions.explanation: He felt embarrassed, but his sister said it was normal.

questions.prompt: What did the writer see through the window?
options: The city getting smaller below him
questions.explanation: The whole city was getting smaller, like a model.

questions.prompt: What happened when the plane landed?
options: He lost his bag in the terminal
His parents bought him a gift
His grandmother was waiting with a sign
questions.explanation: His grandmother was waiting with a huge sign with his name.

questions.prompt: How does the writer feel about flying now?
options: He prefers to travel by train
He is keen to become a pilot
questions.explanation: He wants to become a pilot one day.

parts.title: How to get through the airport quickly
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Airports can be stressful places, but a little preparation makes the experience much easier. [1] Many airlines allow you to check in on your phone the day before, which saves a lot of time.

When you arrive, go straight to the bag drop if you have a suitcase. [2] Remember to check the weight, because heavy bags can be expensive.

At security, be ready. [3] It is also a good idea to wear shoes that are easy to remove. Many people forget this and hold up the queue.

Once you are through, look at the screens to find your gate. [4] However, do not go too far away, as the gate sometimes changes at the last minute. [5] Finally, listen carefully to the speakers, so that you never miss your flight.
sentences: Have your passport and boarding pass in your hand.
Keep your boarding pass in a safe pocket until you board.
There is usually plenty of time to buy a coffee or a book.
The pilot will tell you when it is safe to stand up.
Staff will weigh it and put a label on it.

gaps.explanation: Starting by checking in online matches the next sentence about checking in on your phone.
The bag drop is where staff weigh the suitcase and add a label, and then weight is mentioned.
At security you need your documents ready, and the next sentence adds shoes.
After finding your gate, there is time for a coffee, and then "however" warns about not going far.
Keeping the boarding pass safe is a final tip, and then "Finally" introduces the announcements.

parts.title: A message from the airport
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Hi Tom, I am writing this at the airport. My flight [1] delayed by two hours, so I am sitting in a café. I [2] here since six o'clock this morning. The woman at the desk said that there [3] a problem with the engine. I am quite tired, [4] I have a good book with me. If everything goes well, I [5] home by midnight. I really hope the plane takes off [6] long.

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: Present perfect passive: "has been delayed".

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: "Since six o'clock" needs the present perfect.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: Reported past: "there was a problem".

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: "But" shows contrast: tired, but has a book.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: Future prediction: "will be home".

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: "Before long" means soon.

parts.title: Airport rules for passengers
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Welcome to Bridgeport Airport. Please arrive at least two hours [1] your flight so that you have enough time to check in. All passengers must show [2] passport at the security desk. If you are carrying liquids, they must be [3] a clear plastic bag. Do not leave your bags alone, because security staff may take them [4]. Please switch off your phone [5] you are on the plane. Thank you, and we hope that you [6] a pleasant journey.

gaps.explanation: Liquids must be "in" a clear plastic bag.
We hope that you "have" a pleasant journey.

parts.title: A tour of the airport
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: clara
turns.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to our airport tour. My name's Clara. The tour takes ninety minutes, and we start here in the main hall. First, we will visit the control tower, which is fifty metres high. After that, we will watch the baggage system, which moves nearly ten thousand suitcases every day. Then we go outside to see the fire station, where you can sit in a real fire engine. Lunch is included, and you can choose chicken or fish. The tour costs twelve pounds for adults and is free for children. Please remember to bring your passport to show who you are. Finally, you cannot take photographs in the security area.

gaps.explanation: The control tower is fifty metres high.

gaps.prompt: The baggage system moves nearly ten thousand ___ every day
gaps.explanation: It moves nearly ten thousand suitcases every day.

gaps.prompt: At the fire station, you can sit in a fire ___
gaps.explanation: You can sit in a real fire engine.

gaps.prompt: The tour costs ___ pounds for adults
gaps.explanation: It costs twelve pounds for adults.
Please remember to bring your passport.

parts.title: A pilot
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: Today I'm talking to Jenna Ford, who has been a pilot for fifteen years. Jenna, why did you choose this job?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: My father was a pilot, and when I was small he took me to the airport to see the planes. I never wanted to do anything else.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: What is the best part of your job?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: The view. When you fly above the clouds at sunrise, it is the most beautiful sight in the world. I still look at it every day.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: Is there anything you find difficult?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: Being away from home. Sometimes I'm abroad for five days, and I miss my family. We talk on the phone every night, though.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: Have you ever been frightened?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: Once, when a bird hit the engine just after take-off. We had to return to the airport quickly. Everyone was safe, but I was shaking afterwards.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: What do you do before a flight?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: We check the weather, the route and the fuel together. It takes about an hour, and nothing is left to chance.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: What advice would you give to young people?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: Study hard, especially maths and science, and don't give up. It is a long road, but it's worth every minute.
